question: The challenges linked to the cost of water and sanitation services in Alba County beg the question of equitable access to these basic services. There are significant pricing differences between Alba County and other nearby areas, raising reasonable questions about how the county authorities are spending European money and about their implementation of European rules. Consumers in Alba County pay RON 7.

56 per cubic metre of drinking water and RON 7.86 per cubic metre of wastewater, while consumers in other counties pay much less. While, in the EU, 4 % of the population has limited access to quality drinking water, 21.2 % of Romanians have no access to basic sanitation facilities, compared to the EU average of 1.5 %. The EU has earmarked EUR 10.
8 billion for improvements to drinking water and wastewater infrastructure for the period 2021-2027. 1.
How does the Commission plan to harmonise water resource management standards and practices across Member States to ensure a uniform and sustainable approach in the EU?

How does the Commission plan to monitor and assess efficiency in the use of the funds allocated to Member States to improve water and sanitation services, ensuring that these funds help reduce inequalities and promote access to quality water?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.5.2024) 1. At EU level, the supply of drinking water and management of urban wastewater are governed by the Drinking Water Directive1 and the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive2 respectively. In conformity with the principle of subsidiarity, both Directives do not provide on how Member States should organise their water supply or set water tariffs.

The Water Framework Directive3 sets out specific rules for the protection of surface and groundwater bodies used for abstraction of drinking water. Article 9 obliges Member States to take account of the principle of the recovery of costs of water services. Member States have to establish River Basin Management Plans (RBMPs), including measures to achieve good water status and avoid deterioration.

The Commission is currently assessing the third cycle RBMPs4 and will formulate recommendations to Member States in a report to be adopted in 2024. The Commission offers technical support to Member States5 to implement structural reforms, including in the water sector. 2.

The main EU funding for water supply and wastewater treatment in Romania comes from Romania’s Sustainable Development Programme6, financed by Cohesion Policy funds7, the Recovery and Resilience Plan8, and the National Programme for Rural Development9.

A reform of Law No 241/2006 on water supply and sewerage, including the alignment of the tariff strategy of the regional water and sewerage operator in accordance with EU law, is currently planned. The EU funding10 contributes to promote access to quality water and wastewater treatment services and to reduce inequalities, addressing implementation issues and by monitoring certain indicators, e.g.
in terms of population connected to improved public water supply and waste water treatment.
